questions.q: What term did Bernier use to describe Mughal cities, and what did he imply by it?
questions.a: Bernier called Mughal cities "camp towns" (villes de camp), implying they owed their existence to the imperial camp, flourished only when the court was present, and rapidly declined when it moved — lacking independent economic foundations. A wrong answer (e.g., "manufacturing towns" or "port towns") reveals the student has not grasped Bernier's core thesis about urban dependency on imperial patronage.

questions.q: Why did Bernier argue that artisans had no incentive to improve their craft, and what evidence from his own writing contradicts this pessimism?
questions.a: Bernier claimed profits were appropriated by the state, so artisans in karkhanas worked without aspiration for improvement. However, he simultaneously noted that vast quantities of gold and silver flowed into India because manufactures were exported globally — indicating high demand for Indian crafts. A student who misses the contradiction shows they read Bernier selectively, not critically.

questions.q: Using Bernier's description of imperial karkhanas and the NCERT's mention of merchant organizations (mahajans, nagarsheth), explain why Bernier's "camp towns" model fails to explain the survival of towns like Ahmedabad or Surat when the imperial court was absent.
questions.a: Bernier's karkhanas were state-sponsored workshops serving imperial demand, but Ahmedabad and Surat thrived on merchant networks (mahajans), maritime trade, and textile exports to West Asia and Southeast Asia — independent of court presence. A wrong answer that equates all towns with karkhanas ignores the diversity of urban economic bases (manufacturing, trade, pilgrimage) documented in the same period.

questions.q: How did Bernier's "camp towns" thesis feed into Montesquieu's "oriental despotism" and Marx's "Asiatic mode of production"? Identify the specific chain of intellectual influence.
questions.a: Bernier → Montesquieu (18th century): used crown ownership + camp towns to argue Asian rulers had absolute authority over subjugated subjects. → Marx (19th century): adapted this into Asiatic mode of production — state appropriates surplus from autonomous, egalitarian villages, leading to stagnation. A student who reverses the sequence or attributes "oriental despotism" directly to Marx shows confusion about historiographical genealogy.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Bernier's account is useless for understanding 17th-century Mughal urban economy because of his Eurocentric bias." Provide two pieces of evidence from the text that support AND two that challenge this view.
questions.a: Support: (1) He imposes binary East/West hierarchy; (2) He misreads land revenue as rent. Challenge: (1) His karkhana description is the only detailed contemporary account of workshop organization; (2) He records precious metal inflows and merchant prosperity, contradicting his own decline narrative. A one-sided answer reveals inability to separate observation from interpretation — a key historian's skill.

questions.q: Construct a 150-word argument either defending or refuting the "camp towns" thesis using ONLY evidence available to a 17th-century observer (Bernier, Ibn Battuta's earlier account, Abu'l Fazl's Ain-i-Akbari, European factory records). State your position clearly.
questions.a: A strong answer will: (1) Take a clear stance; (2) Cite at least three specific pieces of evidence (e.g., Bernier's karkhanas vs. Ibn Battuta's Daulatabad bazaar vs. Abu'l Fazl's revenue categories vs. Dutch East India Company procurement records from Surat); (3) Explain why "camp towns" fits some cities (Fatehpur Sikri) but not others (Ahmedabad, Masulipatnam). A weak answer relies on modern generalizations or ignores the temporal gap between Ibn Battuta (14th c.) and Bernier (17th c.).
